thread.title: Market Review And Outlook For August 2018

author: Nasdaq
title: Market Review And Outlook For August 2018
text:
Shutterstock photo U.S. Indices
Executive Summary:
Q2 S&P earnings grew 25% for the second consecutive quarter fueling stock gains. The S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite & 100, and Russell 2000 indexes all hit record highs during August. Leading sectors and indices in August largely continued ongoing YTD trends. Tech, small caps and growth stocks outperformed. Industrials, value and non-U.S. stocks lagged. The U.S. Dollar's strength held steady in August as two additional Fed rate hikes seems the most likely outcome. Global market underperformance, violent FX swings and ongoing trade tensions are potential risks for U.S. stocks. Equity performance was strong in August with most major indices melting up to record highs despite continued concerns surrounding global trade and emerging market pressures. In the final week alone stocks saw a boost following a preliminary trade agreement between the United States and Mexico, NAFTA 2.0. Although an agreement with Canada could not be reached by Trump's self-imposed deadline of August 31st, the White House then said talks will extend into the first week of September as Canada risks losing part of its auto sector focused on U.S. brands. At the same time the administration is in no rush to complete bilateral deals with Europe and China ensuring trade tensions are likely to remain elevated well past the midterm elections. It is reported Trump plans to move forward with tariffs on $200B worth of Chinese goods, possibly as early as this week. And in a Bloomberg interview, the President said the EU's offer to eliminate auto tariffs does not go far enough while comparing their trade policies to those of China. Yet stocks and the U.S. economy continue to benefit from the impact of the tax reform and increased spending.
The second estimate of Q2 GDP was revised higher (+4.2% actual vs. 4.1% prior and 4% consensus) which along with other economic data all but guarantees a September rate hike. A fourth rate hike in December is more likely than not with markets now pricing in a 63% probability, according to Bloomberg. Economic data, policy mix, and interest rate differentials continue to support a stronger US dollar. The US dollar Index (DXY) registered its fifth consecutive monthly gain in August for the first time since 2014 when it then recorded nine consecutive months in the green ending March 2015. And now with the administration considering indexing capital gains taxes to inflation, synonymous to a tax cut, monetary policy should continue to become gradually less accommodative. While the U.S. is seemingly firing on all cylinders, the same cannot be said for the rest of the world which in some parts is going through a period of deep risk aversion.
The Nasdaq 100 and Composite once again led all major indices in monthly performance with a gain of 5.8% and 5.7% in August, followed by 4.2% gains in both smaller cap Russell 2000 and Microcap indices. The S&P 500 and 400 (midcap) indices each posted gains of 3%, while the blue chip Dow Industrials brought up the rear with a return of 2.2%. As seen in the performance table, the performance rankings in August are nearly identical with the YTD rankings. With 2/3 of 2018 in the books, the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 and Composite indices are leading with YTD gains of 19.7% and 17.5% as the Dow Industrials is the worst relative performer, +5% YTD. Growth continues to meaningfully outperform.
Longest running bull market … Last month was the best August in terms of price performance since 2014. On August 22 nd the S&P 500 closed at 2,861.82 marking the longest bull market in history as measured by some - 3,453 days without a 20% or greater decline. The index closed at 676.53 on March 9, 2009, rising more than 320% through the close on 8/22. The current bull market eclipsed for length the previous bull-market record that ran from October 1990 to the bursting of the tech bubble in March 2000. However, the market gained more, 417%, over that 3,452-day period. In August, the S&P hit an all-time intra-day high of 2873.23.
August gains continued after 8/22 with the S&P 500, Russell 2000 and Nasdaq Composite each hitting new record highs for four successive days ending 8/29 and closing the month with respective gains of 3.0%, 4.5% and 5.7%. The Nasdaq 100 also hit a record high in August and led the major indices with a 5.8% gain. Notably, the Dow, which outperformed earlier in the year, has been lagging in part due to its underweight in tech and overweigh in industrials relative to the others. AAPL, the most heavily weighted stock in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Indexes, ended August at a record high after surpassing $1 trillion in market cap. BA, the most heavily weighted stock in the Dow Industrials, underperformed.
S&P GICS Sectors
While the Information Technology sector rebounded sharply in August from a relatively weaker July, there remain some macro concerns that could affect the market as a whole and the sector specifically. On the positive side, tech sector earnings in Q2 finished at a beat rate of 89% surpassing 80% beat rates for the S&P 500 overall. This is all the more impressive since the 80% beat rates was the highest since FactSet began compiling data in 2008. On a pure performance measure, Information Technology as a whole gained 6.7% despite an early month downgrade of the Semi space by Morgan Stanley. Within the category the Technology Hardware and Equipment sector rose 15.6% while Software and Services gained 4.4% and Semi and Semi Equipment increased 2.8%.
Fun fact: Since closing with a market cap above the widely watched $1 trillion mark on 8/2, AAPL has quietly added an additional $99.4 billion to its market cap, about the same as Starbucks and Ingersoll-Rand combined .
While there is still a great deal of optimism regarding the sector's growth, there are lingering concerns that have investors cautious. Competition globally, especially from areas with low labor costs, will likely continue to compress profit margins. If trade conflicts escalate it could raise costs for U.S. producers and prices for consumers. We continue to see signs that companies remain hesitant to increase capital investment beyond what is absolutely necessary, although there are signs that is beginning to end.
Finally the upcoming changes in the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) framework (discussed below) could result in some volatility, as the tech sector is estimated to move from 26% of the S&P 500 index weight to around 21%. Despite these investor concerns, the fundamentals in the sector remain strong. Balance sheets appear solid, with large cash balances and relatively low debt. In addition we have seen tech sector companies increase their dividend payments which may become a larger part of total equity return in the near term. They also have also increased share buyback programs
Consumer Strength: Consumer Discretionary names had a strong August following a bevy of earnings reports in the last two weeks of the month. The S&P 500 Retail Index gained 8.3% for August, and more than 33% since the April lows. This helped push the broader based S&P 500 Consumer Discretionary Index up 5% for August and 19.9% from its April lows. AMZN's strong performance and significant weight in this index also helps. Consumer spending is an important factor in U.S. GDP and any signs of strength there should be viewed as a positive for the economy while any weakness should be cause for concern. The Discretionary Index finished August with an 18.3% gain YTD. And while the strong performance may be attributable to a few large cap weighted members, the below chart of the S&P 500 Consumer Discretionary Equal Weight Index shows a bullish "cup and handle" continuation pattern forming since the January highs. A breakout above the "neckline" projects a measured move to 4,160, +10.5% from current levels.
A Healthy Market: Healthcare stocks have had a strong summer. The S&P 500 Healthcare Index (S5HLTH) returned 4.2% for August and is the best performing sector over the last 2 months. The S5HLTH Index is the best performing index since Memorial Day, gaining 11.8% since the holiday. Not to be outdone, the Nasdaq Biotech Index (NBI) returned 4.8% in August and 13.7% since Memorial Day. The S&P 500 Index has returned just over 3% for August and only 6.6% since Memorial Day.
S&P is launching a new Communications Services sector this fall that will replace the outdated Telecommunications sector and shuffle a number of companies into new sectors. The classification changes go into effect at the close on Friday September 21 st for S&P with MSCI following Suit in December, impacting a great many indexes and related funds/ETFs. Analysts see little immediate impact, instead they expect fund managers will adjust their positions over time. There was a similar change two years ago when REITs were carved out from the financial sector and established as a standalone sector. Although smaller in scale, it was a nonevent from a trade standpoint. September 21st is also quad-witching and the standard quarterly rebalance of the S&P indexes.
Bernstein provides this overview : This renamed sector will include existing telecom companies (such as T, VZ, TMU.S.), plus firms selected from the Consumer Discretionary Sector (including NFLX, DIS, CMCSA, and TWX) and the Information Technology sector (including FB, GOOG, TWTR , EA and ATVI) to better reflect communications, media and entertainment and how these groups have evolved over time. Meanwhile other adjustments include moving e-commerce companies like EBAY, GRUB, and ETSY from Technology to Consumer Discretionary. The new Communications sector jumps to 10% of S&P 500 market capitalization from the old Telecom weight of 2%, while Technology shrinks from 26% to 21%and Consumer Discretionary goes from 13% to 11% of the index.
Global Indices
Global indices representing many of the world's largest economies are meaningfully underperforming the U.S. and in many cases stand in the red on a YTD basis. China's Shanghai Composite (SHCOMP) declined 5.3% in August. From its January highs to August lows the SHCOMP gave back more than 26% and is down 17.6% YTD ending August. Japan's Nikkei finished with a monthly gain of 1.4% but is barely positive YTD, +0.4%. Germany and the United Kingdom declined 3.4% and 4.1% in August. Both indices saw double digit declines in Q2 and now stand in the red YTD with declines of 4.3% and 3.3%. One of the few bright spots is India whose Nifty index gained 2.9% in August and is now up 10.9% YTD.
As previously noted economic data, monetary policy mix, and interest rate differentials are driving U.S. dollar strength relative to most global currencies. While the dollar index (DXY) was forming a streak of five consecutive months in the green, we noted in the August 16 daily MID BLOG that the DXY was showing technical signs of exhaustion and thus an intermediate term top could already be underway. Looking back the dollar's high was made in the prior session, August 15 th , and was then followed by three consecutive weekly declines. It now appears this correction is complete and the longer term uptrend has resumed. Last week's close, $95.14, finished within a penny of our $95.15 expectation. Also, the weekly price action formed a bullish "doji" pattern which is seeing upside confirmation on the first session in September. While a full week of data is required for official confirmation, the price action is thus far promising for bulls.
Economy:
The second read for 2Q GDP on 8/29 showed that the economy grew by 4.2%, higher than the initial report of 4.1% growth and a 4.0% estimate. Personal Consumption rose 3.8%, one of the best readings in many years but lower than the survey estimate of 3.9%. With corporate earnings growing at 25% in the first and second quarters and the Fed expected to continue along its normalization path, nothing in these releases moved the needle on Wall Street. The question still remains how long can the economy expand at current rates and will this translate into 2019 earnings growth that will be enough to support valuations. Forward P/E's are currently a reasonable 16.5 times, especially considering that the 10-year treasury yield is below 3%. Right now the market seems happy with the economic situation right now.
Earnings:
We focus a lot in this note about S&P 500 earnings growth, which has been stellar. 1Q earnings grew 24.8%, followed by 25% growth in Q2 - the highest growth since Q3 2010. Heading into Q2, earnings were expected to grow at "only" about 20% and some investors were concerned that 1Q might represent the peak. The better than expected growth explains in large measure why the market has rallied to new highs in August. Also, in Q2, 80% of companies beat EPS estimates, the highest beat rate since FactSet began tracking this metric in 2008.
If we look at smaller companies, the story gets even better. Based on data from 90% of Russell 2000 companies that reported in Q2, R2K companies grew earnings at 35% y/y, with sales growth of 10.5%. This is higher than the S&P's 25% earnings growth and 10% sales growth.
S&P 500 companies derive about 30% of revenue from outside the U.S., while Russell 2000 companies have foreign exposure of about 21%, according to Bank of America Merrill Lynch research.
We took a look at approximate non-U.S. revenue by S&P 500 sector on the chart below. As you can see, tech is the most exposed to dollar strength, with over half of revenues coming from overseas. Should the dollar continue to rise, tech, materials, industrials and even healthcare companies could see headwinds to Q3 earnings based on currency conversions and price pressures.
A pretty average summer
It's not surprising that volumes slowed in August as consolidated trading is generally lighter at this time of year due to vacations and the light earnings calendars. The VIX product blow-ups (Feb.) and Italy's political drama (May) are behind us. While August is no stranger to market moving events and thus strong volumes (most recently 2015 due to China devaluation), August 2018 was relatively muted. Below is a chart of trading volume for all U.S. exchange traded stocks this month. Only two days saw volumes above the YTD average of 6.9 billion shares despite a great many trade/tariff headlines which seems to indicate the market is taking this in stride.
Looking ahead:
After two quarters of 25% earnings growth, valuations have moved from over 19X earnings at the beginning of the year to about 16.5X earnings helping equities achieve new highs in August.
A few items to keep on the early warning radar are the $177B in outflows from long only fund managers in Q2, trade concerns, emerging market currencies, Brexit and U.S. midterm elections, all of which would could ding equities if they take on­ more significance than has been priced in by investors so far. Given the relative strength of the U.S. economy, investors seem to be pretty patient around international trade and currency issues. One gets the sense the market is afraid to be short in case the trade issues are resolved. That could change rapidly with one tweet however. Global market underperformance, violent FX swings and new trade tensions are also risks for U.S. stocks.
